result: V2a neurons in larval zebrafish are divided into at least two morphological subtypes (descending V2a-D and bifurcating V2a-B) that can be distinguished by GFP expression levels, soma size, and mediolateral (ML) position in the spinal cord. High GFP neurons are V2a-Ds and low GFP neurons are V2a-Bs, with V2a-Ds occupying more lateral positions despite similar dorsoventral distributions.
evaluation: Claims C40-C44 and C49-C51 provide converging anatomical and imaging evidence from confocal microscopy and post-hoc fills that consistently demonstrate morphological differences between V2a subtypes. Statistical analyses confirm significant differences in ML position (C44) while showing no significant differences in DV distribution (C42) or number per segment (C43), supporting the anatomical characterization.

result: Descending V2a-D neurons exhibit intrinsic cellular properties suitable for rhythmogenesis at the speeds where they are recruited. Tonic V2a-Ds recruited at fast speeds (>30 Hz) show tonic firing at 40-200 Hz, while bursting V2a-Ds recruited at slow speeds (<30 Hz) show bursting at those frequencies. The correspondence between step-firing and swim-firing patterns is remarkable for V2a-Ds but less obvious for V2a-B neurons.
evaluation: Claims C53-C69 provide extensive current-clamp data showing that intrinsic firing properties of V2a-D neurons match their recruitment frequencies during swimming (C68-C69), with statistical correlations supporting this correspondence. The data demonstrate that V2a-D neurons possess rhythmogenic properties appropriate for their recruitment speeds, while V2a-B neurons lack this correspondence (C70-C71), supporting distinct functional roles.

result: Bifurcating V2a-B neurons are recruited more reliably across all speeds compared to V2a-D neurons, which fire more sparsely and in a stricter modular fashion. Fast V2a-B neurons reach 100% recruitment reliability above 35 Hz, while slow V2a-B neurons maintain 100% reliability below 35 Hz. V2a-D neurons show maximum 50% recruitment reliability in their respective speed ranges.
evaluation: Claims C76-C87 provide cell-attached and voltage-clamp recordings demonstrating clear differences in recruitment patterns between V2a-D and V2a-B neurons across frequency ranges. Statistical analyses (C84-C87) confirm significant differences in recruitment probability, with V2a-B neurons firing significantly more spikes per burst (C93). The data consistently support the pattern-forming role of V2a-B neurons downstream of rhythmogenic V2a-D neurons.

result: At fast speeds, reciprocal (anti-phase) inhibition in descending V2a-D neurons supports phasic firing and rhythmogenesis, while recurrent (in-phase) inhibition in bifurcating V2a-B neurons helps pattern motor output. Fast V2a-Ds receive broadly distributed phasic inhibition with anti-phase peaks, while fast V2a-Bs receive both in-phase and anti-phase inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C96-C120 provide voltage-clamp recordings showing distinct patterns of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents at fast speeds. The phase analysis (C111-C117) demonstrates that fast V2a-Ds receive predominantly reciprocal inhibition while fast V2a-Bs receive both reciprocal and recurrent inhibition. The timing and amplitude of synaptic currents (C99-C106) support the proposed functional roles, with maximum inhibition orders of magnitude larger than excitation, emphasizing the critical role of inhibition timing.

result: At slow speeds, recurrent (in-phase) inhibition in descending V2a-D neurons supports phasic firing and rhythmogenesis, while bifurcating V2a-B neurons rely predominantly on reciprocal (anti-phase) inhibition to pattern output. Slow V2a-Ds show two clear peaks in phasic inhibition (in-phase and anti-phase), while slow V2a-Bs receive predominantly anti-phase inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C107-C108 and C116-C121 provide voltage-clamp data showing that the dominant mode of inhibition is flipped at slow speeds compared to fast speeds. The phase analysis demonstrates coherent peaks in both reciprocal and recurrent inhibition for slow V2a-Ds at slow speeds (C121), while slow V2a-Bs receive predominantly reciprocal inhibition (C118). This cell-type-specific and speed-dependent pattern of inhibition is well-documented across multiple neurons.

result: Synaptic silencing of commissural dI6 neurons using botulinum toxin disrupts rhythmogenesis at fast speeds (causing synchronous bilateral activity) but primarily affects motor output patterning at slow speeds (increasing burst duration and duty cycle without affecting frequency or phase). This supports the conclusion that reciprocal inhibition plays a dominant role in rhythm generation at fast speeds and pattern formation at slow speeds.
evaluation: Claims C130-C142 provide genetic silencing experiments with clear phenotypic outcomes. The data show that dI6 silencing causes loss of left-right alternation at high frequencies (C132-C134) but maintains normal frequency and phase at low frequencies while increasing duty cycle (C137-C139). The differential effects at fast versus slow speeds (C136, C141) support the proposed speed-dependent roles of reciprocal inhibition. The inference that reciprocal inhibition near the hindbrain/spinal cord is essential for high-frequency rhythms (C161) is reasonable given the comparison to prior ablation studies.

result: Cell-type-specific, not common, modes of rhythmogenesis generate and coordinate different speeds of locomotion. All V2a neurons rely on phasic excitation and inhibition to sculpt rhythmic firing, but the specific patterns of synaptic drive vary by cell type and speed in a manner consistent with hierarchical organization and speed modularity.
evaluation: This is the main conclusion synthesizing all experimental findings. Claims C123-C126 provide interpretations of the phase analysis data showing that V2a-D neurons receive excitation earlier than V2a-B neurons (supporting hierarchical organization), and that the coherence of synaptic drive at different frequencies supports speed modularity. The conclusion that common mechanisms are insufficient (C184) is well-supported by the extensive evidence of cell-type-specific and speed-dependent differences in both intrinsic properties and synaptic drive patterns.

result: Prior work has established that V2a neurons are organized into fast/slow subtypes based on DV position and birth order, with V2a-D neurons providing stronger inputs to premotor interneurons and V2a-B neurons providing stronger inputs to motor neurons. Fast V2a-D neurons have longer intersegmental axons and form stronger connections with other V2a neurons, while V2a-B neurons have faster membrane time constants and more reliable motor neuron connections.
evaluation: These claims (C35-C39, C147-C151) summarize prior work from the same laboratory and are appropriately cited. The citations appear accurate and the characterizations are consistent with the referenced studies. This prior work provides essential context for interpreting the current findings.

result: During fictive escape swimming evoked by electrical stimulation, zebrafish show a deceleration pattern with highest frequencies (>60 Hz) at the beginning of the first swim episode (Swim 1), followed by lower and more variable frequencies in subsequent episodes (Swim 2+). This pattern mirrors real swimming behavior.
evaluation: Claims C45-C48 describe the basic swimming behavior used throughout the study. The deceleration pattern is documented in ventral rootlet recordings (C46) and supported by prior citations (C45, C47). This establishes the experimental paradigm for all subsequent recordings.

result: V2a neurons show properties consistent with their proposed roles: median spike distributions occur in advance of motor burst centers (as expected for premotor excitatory interneurons), V2a-B neurons fire slightly before V2a-Ds (consistent with size-related time constants), and spike rates during swimming (200-600 Hz) overlap with rates observed during current steps at 1-2x rheobase.
evaluation: Claims C82-C92 provide supporting evidence linking intrinsic properties to functional recruitment. The spike timing data (C82-C83) and spike rate comparisons (C88-C91) are well-documented and support the functional relevance of the current-clamp measurements. The observation that spike numbers decrease at higher frequencies (C92) is explained by shorter cycle periods.

result: Peak excitatory and inhibitory drive to V2a neurons is normalized to cellular excitability, with lower resistance neurons receiving orders of magnitude more current than higher resistance neurons. Maximum inhibition is orders of magnitude larger than maximum excitation, suggesting that the timing of inhibition plays a critical role in shaping rhythmic output.
evaluation: Claims C99-C104 and C109 demonstrate significant negative correlations between maximum current and input resistance for both excitation and inhibition. The observation that inhibition greatly exceeds excitation (C109) is well-documented and leads to the reasonable inference that inhibition timing is critical (C110). This normalization to excitability is consistent with prior work (C101).

result: The timing of phasic excitation is consistent with hierarchical organization of V2a neurons (V2a-Ds upstream of V2a-Bs), and the presence of in-phase inhibition is associated with more coherent spike distributions in slow V2a-Ds and fast V2a-Bs.
evaluation: Claims C112-C114 show that V2a-D neurons receive excitation earlier than V2a-B neurons, supporting hierarchical organization. Claim C119 links in-phase inhibition to spike coherence. These are reasonable interpretations of the phase distribution data, though they represent inferences rather than direct demonstrations of causality.

result: The initial hypothesis was that cellular properties would be more important for rhythmogenesis at slow speeds while synaptic drive would dominate at fast speeds. However, the findings show that phasic firing in both V2a-Ds and V2a-Bs is best explained by phasic patterns of synaptic excitation and inhibition, suggesting rhythms are generated by more rostral V2a-Ds where rhythmic excitation originates.
evaluation: Claim C152 states the initial hypothesis based on prior motor neuron work. Claims C153-C154 document the intrinsic properties of V2a-D neurons. Claim C155 presents the surprising finding that synaptic drive is critical for all V2a neurons. The inference that rhythms originate rostrally (C156) is reasonable given that phasic excitation is already rhythmic when it arrives at midbody neurons. This is supported by prior optogenetic and lesion studies (C157-C158).

result: The current synaptic silencing strategy included dI6 neurons extending into the hindbrain, unlike prior ablation studies that were limited to spinal dI6 neurons. This difference may explain why the current study shows disruption of fast swimming while prior ablation studies did not.
evaluation: Claim C159 accurately cites prior work showing that spinal dI6 ablation does not prevent fast swimming. Claim C160 documents that the current strategy included hindbrain dI6 neurons. This comparison is appropriate and helps explain the different outcomes, though the authors acknowledge other potential differences between ablation and silencing approaches.

result: The proposed model suggests that slow and fast modules have mirror-image wiring diagrams with type I V2a-D neurons providing rhythmogenesis and type II V2a-B neurons providing pattern formation. In the fast module, rhythmogenesis relies on reciprocal inhibition while recurrent inhibition limits motor output. In the slow module, recurrent inhibition supports rhythmogenesis in V2a-Ds while reciprocal inhibition patterns activity in V2a-Bs.
evaluation: Claims C162-C175 present a comprehensive model integrating all experimental findings. The model is well-supported by the data showing cell-type-specific and speed-dependent patterns of inhibition. The citations to prior work in lampreys and frogs (C169-C171) appropriately contextualize the findings. The model represents a reasonable synthesis of the experimental evidence, though it remains a proposed framework requiring further testing.

result: Background claims about vertebrate locomotion, historical theories of rhythmogenesis, zebrafish swimming modes, motor neuron organization, and comparisons to other systems and life stages provide context for the current findings.
evaluation: These claims (C11-C29, C140, C143-C146, C176-C183) provide background information and context, all appropriately cited. The characterizations of prior work and general principles appear accurate. These claims establish the scientific context but do not represent novel findings from the current study.

result: Spinal motor neurons exhibit a range of rhythmogenic cellular properties that likely contribute to the higher-frequency bursts observed unilaterally during dI6 silencing experiments.
evaluation: Claim C135 cites prior work showing that motor neurons have rhythmogenic properties. This is used to explain the observation of unilateral high-frequency bursting during bilateral synchrony in dI6 BoTx-GFP fish. The explanation is reasonable and appropriately cited.
